subject: social
title: Social Studies Book — M/J World History (Grade 6)
intro: Travel back in time to meet the first humans and the amazing ancient civilizations that built the world we live in today!

lessons.title: Time, Timelines, and Eras
lessons.teach: Historians put events in order from oldest to newest using timelines. They also use time words like decade (10 years), century (100 years), and millennium (1,000 years). 'BC/BCE' means before the year zero and counts backward, while 'AD/CE' counts forward — so 500 BC happened before 500 AD.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
lessons.teach: A primary source comes straight from the time being studied, like a diary, a clay tablet, or an old coin. A secondary source is made later by someone who studied those clues, like a textbook or a museum sign. Historians use both, but primary sources give the most direct evidence about the past.

lessons.title: How Historians Investigate the Past
lessons.teach: Historical inquiry means asking questions about the past and hunting for evidence to answer them, almost like being a detective. Historians compare different sources, look for who made them and why, and notice that two people can describe the same event differently. History also connects to other subjects like geography, economics, and government.

lessons.title: Latitude, Longitude, and Map Tools
lessons.teach: Maps use a grid of lines to find any spot on Earth: latitude lines run east-west and measure how far north or south you are, while longitude lines run north-south and measure how far east or west you are. Where two lines cross gives an exact location. Geographers also use scale, a compass rose, and special maps to study the world.
lessons.videoTitle: Map skills / latitude & longitude — Miacademy Learning Channel

lessons.title: Types of Maps and Map Projections
lessons.teach: Because Earth is round and maps are flat, every map projection stretches or shrinks parts of the world a little. Political maps show borders and cities, physical maps show landforms like mountains and rivers, and special-purpose maps show things like climate or population. You pick the map that best fits the question you are asking.

lessons.title: Rivers, Seas, and Where People Settle
lessons.teach: Major bodies of water shaped where early people built their homes. Rivers gave fresh water for drinking and farming, and seas became highways for trade and travel. That is why so many of the world's first civilizations grew right beside rivers and along coastlines.

lessons.title: Cultural Diffusion: How Ideas Spread
lessons.teach: Cultural diffusion is the spreading of ideas, goods, religions, and inventions from one group of people to another. It happened through trade, travel, migration, and even war. This is how things like the alphabet, new foods, and beliefs moved from one ancient civilization to the next.

topics.title: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution

lessons.title: Hunter-Gatherers vs. Early Farmers
lessons.teach: For most of human history, people were hunter-gatherers who moved around to hunt animals and gather wild plants. About 10,000 years ago, some groups learned to plant crops and raise animals, so they could stay in one place. This new farming life let people store food, build permanent homes, and grow into larger communities.
lessons.videoTitle: Early humans / agricultural revolution — Crash Course World History #1

lessons.title: Farming, Metal Tools, and the Rise of Civilization
lessons.teach: When farming produced extra food, not everyone had to grow crops, so people could become builders, priests, traders, or leaders. Learning to work metals like bronze gave stronger tools and weapons. These changes led to bigger populations, towns, and eventually the first civilizations.

lessons.title: The Characteristics of a Civilization
lessons.teach: A civilization is more than just a big group of people — it usually has cities, organized government, a writing system, specialized jobs, social classes, and a shared religion or culture. Spotting these features helps us tell a true civilization apart from a small village. Early river valleys had all of these traits.

lessons.title: Tracing Early Human Migration
lessons.teach: Archaeologists find the oldest evidence of humans in Africa and Asia, then trace how people slowly migrated across the whole planet. By following bones, tools, and cave art, scientists can map the routes early humans took. These migrations spread people, and their cultures, to nearly every continent.

lessons.title: The Land Between Two Rivers
lessons.teach: Mesopotamia means 'land between the rivers,' sitting between the Tigris and Euphrates in the Middle East. The rivers flooded and left rich soil, making it great for farming — people even called this area the Fertile Crescent. This good land helped one of the world's first civilizations grow here.

lessons.title: Achievements: Writing, Wheel, and Cities
lessons.teach: The Sumerians of Mesopotamia gave the world some huge 'firsts,' including cuneiform — one of the earliest writing systems made by pressing wedges into clay. They also built the first cities, used the wheel, and created early math based on the number 60 (which is why we still have 60-minute hours). These inventions shaped civilizations for thousands of years.

lessons.title: Hammurabi and His Famous Code
lessons.teach: Hammurabi was a Babylonian king who wrote down one of the first sets of laws, called the Code of Hammurabi, and carved it on a tall stone for everyone to see. The laws followed the idea of 'an eye for an eye,' so punishments matched the crime. Writing laws down meant rules applied to everyone, not just whatever a ruler felt like that day.

lessons.title: The Israelites and Monotheism
lessons.teach: The ancient Israelites were special because they believed in just one God, an idea called monotheism, while most neighbors worshipped many gods. Their beliefs and stories were written in their sacred texts and stressed following moral laws like the Ten Commandments. This idea of one God later shaped Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

lessons.title: The Gift of the Nile
lessons.teach: Egypt grew along the Nile River, which flooded each year and left behind rich black soil perfect for farming. The desert around Egypt acted like a natural wall, protecting it from invaders. Because the Nile was so important, the Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile.'
lessons.videoTitle: Ancient Egypt — Crash Course World History #4

lessons.title: Pyramids, Hieroglyphics, and Achievements
lessons.teach: The Egyptians built enormous stone pyramids as tombs for their pharaohs and created a picture-writing system called hieroglyphics. They were skilled in medicine, math, and engineering, and invented papyrus, an early kind of paper. Many of their achievements still amaze scientists today.

lessons.title: Pharaohs and Key Figures of Egypt
lessons.teach: Egypt was ruled by pharaohs, kings who were seen as god-like leaders. Famous figures include King Tutankhamun, whose untouched tomb was discovered in 1922, and Hatshepsut, one of the few female pharaohs. These leaders organized building projects, armies, and trade.

lessons.title: The Indus Valley Civilization
lessons.teach: One of the earliest civilizations grew in the Indus River Valley in what is now Pakistan and India. Cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro had advanced features like brick houses, straight streets, and even indoor plumbing and sewer systems. Their planning shows how organized this ancient society was.
lessons.videoTitle: Ancient India (Indus Valley) — Crash Course World History #2

lessons.title: Aryan Migrations and the Caste System
lessons.teach: After the Indus cities declined, groups called the Aryans migrated into India and shaped its language and culture. Society became divided into ranked groups called the caste system, where the family you were born into decided your role in life. People generally could not move from one caste to another.

lessons.title: Hinduism and Buddhism
lessons.teach: Hinduism is one of the world's oldest religions, teaching ideas like karma, reincarnation, and many gods who are seen as forms of one spirit. Buddhism began when a prince named Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught that letting go of selfish desire leads to peace. Both religions started in India and spread across Asia.

lessons.title: The Mauryan and Gupta Empires
lessons.teach: The Mauryan Empire united much of India, and its greatest ruler, Asoka, spread Buddhism and ideas of peace after a terrible war. Later, the Gupta Empire is often called India's 'Golden Age' because of advances in math, science, and art. Gupta thinkers helped create the number zero and our modern number symbols.

lessons.title: Rivers, Dynasties, and the Mandate of Heaven
lessons.teach: Chinese civilization grew along the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers and was ruled by families called dynasties. The Chinese believed in the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven gave a ruler the right to rule only as long as he ruled wisely and fairly. If a dynasty became cruel or weak, people believed it lost the mandate and could be replaced.
lessons.videoTitle: Ancient China — Crash Course World History #7

lessons.title: Confucius, Laozi, and Chinese Thinkers
lessons.teach: Ancient China produced famous teachers whose ideas guided life for centuries. Confucius taught respect, good manners, and that leaders should set a good example, while Laozi (Daoism) taught living simply and in harmony with nature. Han Fei Zi taught Legalism, the belief that strict laws and harsh punishments keep order.

lessons.title: Inventions and the Silk Roads
lessons.teach: China invented paper, silk, the compass, and gunpowder, plus they built the Great Wall to defend their land. The Silk Roads were long trade routes that carried Chinese silk west and brought new goods and ideas back east. These routes connected China, India, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean world.

lessons.title: The Mongol Empire
lessons.teach: The Mongols, led by Genghis Khan, built the largest connected land empire in history by conquering across Asia and into Europe. His grandson Kublai Khan ruled China and welcomed traders and travelers like Marco Polo. Mongol control made the Silk Roads safer, which helped trade and ideas spread even farther.

lessons.title: City-States and the Birth of Democracy
lessons.teach: Greece was made of independent city-states called a polis, each with its own government. Athens created an early form of democracy, where citizens could vote on laws and take part in government — though women, enslaved people, and foreigners could not vote. These Greek ideas about voting and rule of law influence governments around the world today.
lessons.videoTitle: Ancient Greece (Persians & Greeks) — Crash Course World History #5

lessons.title: Athens vs. Sparta
lessons.teach: Athens and Sparta were the two most famous Greek city-states, and they were very different. Athens valued education, art, and democracy, while Sparta focused almost entirely on training tough soldiers from a young age. Comparing them shows how two neighbors could build very different ways of life.

lessons.title: The Persian and Peloponnesian Wars
lessons.teach: When the huge Persian Empire invaded, the Greek city-states united and won surprising victories at battles like Marathon and Salamis. Later, Athens and Sparta turned on each other in the long Peloponnesian War, which weakened Greece. These wars show both the strength of Greek teamwork and the danger of fighting among themselves.

lessons.title: Greek Achievements and the Hellenistic Age
lessons.teach: The Greeks gave the world philosophy (thinkers like Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle), theater, the Olympics, and ideas in math and science. Alexander the Great then conquered a huge empire and spread Greek culture across the Middle East and Asia, beginning the Hellenistic Age. This blending of Greek and Eastern cultures shaped the ancient world for centuries.

lessons.title: The Roman Republic
lessons.teach: Rome began as a republic, a government where citizens elected leaders called senators to make decisions for them. The Romans created a system with separation of powers and the rule of law, ideas that influenced later governments, including the United States. Roman citizens were also expected to take part in their government, a duty called civic duty.
lessons.videoTitle: Ancient Rome — Crash Course World History #10

lessons.title: The Punic Wars and Roman Expansion
lessons.teach: Rome and the city of Carthage fought three brutal wars called the Punic Wars over control of the Mediterranean. Carthage's general Hannibal famously marched elephants over the mountains, but Rome won in the end and destroyed Carthage. These victories turned Rome into the master of the Mediterranean and set the stage for a mighty empire.

lessons.title: From Republic to Empire
lessons.teach: As Rome grew, its republic struggled, and a general named Julius Caesar took control before being assassinated. His heir Augustus became the first emperor, beginning the Roman Empire and a long period of peace called the Pax Romana. Power shifted from elected leaders to one powerful emperor.

lessons.title: Roman Achievements and Early Christianity
lessons.teach: Romans were master builders, creating roads, aqueducts that carried water, concrete buildings, and laws that still shape the world. During the empire, Christianity began in Roman lands, teaching belief in one God and Jesus, and slowly spread until it became the empire's main religion. Roman roads and trade actually helped these new ideas travel quickly.

lessons.title: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
lessons.teach: After the Pax Romana, the western half of the Roman Empire slowly declined over many years. Causes included weak leaders, money problems, a huge size that was hard to defend, and invasions by outside groups. By 476 AD the Western Roman Empire had fallen, ending the ancient classical world in Europe.

lessons.title: The Kingdoms of Kush and Axum
lessons.teach: South of Egypt along the Nile rose the kingdom of Kush, which traded gold, ivory, and iron and even ruled Egypt for a time. Later the kingdom of Axum in East Africa became a powerful trading center and was one of the first kingdoms to adopt Christianity. These African kingdoms show that great civilizations grew across the whole continent.

lessons.title: Trade, Barter, and Money in the Ancient World
lessons.teach: Long ago people traded by barter, swapping goods directly, like trading grain for cloth. Over time civilizations created money, such as coins, as a medium of exchange that made trading much easier. Trade connected distant regions, spreading not just goods but also ideas and inventions.

lessons.title: Scarcity, Supply, and Economic Choices
lessons.teach: Scarcity means there is never enough of everything people want, so societies must make choices about how to use resources like land, labor, and tools. Choosing one thing means giving up another, which is called opportunity cost. Ancient civilizations used trade and new technology to deal with scarcity and grow their economies.
